content.fullText:
[00:01] In this lesson, I want to draw your attention to a very challenging scenario that, unfortunately, is not rare in the markets.
[00:09] The idea here is to explore the different tactics you can employ in order to avoid trading incorrectly in such scenario.
[00:17] In this chart, you can see that I highlighted higher highs and higher lows. And in each low, I marked the lines that come out of the DFBs and DFS patterns, which are used to draw demand zones in this case.
[00:29] Every time price comes back to the previous demand zone, it produces the beginning of a new upward price vector that leads to a subsequent higher high.
[00:38] This pattern cannot continue forever, and in the last demand zone, we can see that price simply ignores the zone completely.
[00:47] This relates to a very important point regarding zones, lines, or any type of price barrier, which is that the trader must observe if price indeed reacts to the lines that were previously drawn.
[00:59] Trusting lines without seeing if price will react to them is usually a dangerous exercise that can result in many unnecessary losses.
[01:08] This is partly why intrinsic properties are so important. They are going to tell you if price is reacting appropriately to a price barrier.
[01:17] From the point of view of phase analysis, in this next chart you can see that I marked a possible Elliott wave count of this market.
[01:25] Notice how we can spot five main waves and five waves within wave three.
[01:30] The reason I'm employing phase analysis here is because the completion of five waves suggests a greater retracement that might violate the last demand zone in this case.
[01:41] This is a second indication you can look for in situations like this. Notice how the current price action is poking the red wave four and the blue waves two and four on a slightly smaller scale.
[01:53] The question here is when this market movement is going to stop. Notice also that wave four is not supposed to retrace back into wave one, but that's an arbitrary rule of Elliott Wave. Most people will simply react to the perception of five obvious waves.
[02:11] Another important tip is to observe what the current minor flow is doing instead of trying to pick one previous demand zone to trust.
[02:19] Moving a few candles into the future, we can see the development of the minor flow. A lower low is produced in the form of a bear trap, judging by the fact that these candles fail to close below the last minor low.
[02:32] Let's take a moment here to analyze the intrinsic properties of the candlestick that produces the bear trap to begin with.
[02:40] We see a bearish wide range candle with medium body percentage and a body positioned in the upper range. The prominent lower shadows provide the impression of buying pressure, but at the same time, we have a bearish bias in this candle. Price is also touching what used to be the demand zone in the same way it would do with the traditional support and resistance line.
[03:02] In summary, we have mixed signals in a situation like this. So the best alternative is to wait for price to do something less unpredictable.
[03:12] In this next chart, we can see that after the bear trap, the minor flow begins to go up, and the demand zone that was violated becomes relevant once again. On top of that, price returns to an easily recognizable support line.
[03:27] There are other ways of knowing that the bear trap was indeed a market edge. One of them is through the use of pitchforks, for example. The most obvious one we can draw here is this. The bear trap touches the lower line of the fork without violating it. We can use the same axis to draw a modified Schiff with a double line to the downside, and we'll notice that the lower line of this fork catches the lower tails of those candles in a suggestive manner.
[03:56] Moving price forward, we can see that the minor flow to the upside continues. Notice how price comes back to the reclaimed demand zone once again before moving to the upside to meet the major high.
[04:07] You will often find yourself in situations like this where you are expecting the major points of the market to produce a reaction while the minor flow is giving you the hints of what's going to happen.

keyEvents.description: The initial chart shows a clear uptrend with higher highs and higher lows marked by a zig-zag line. Three distinct grey rectangles are drawn, highlighting demand zones at each higher low, which are respected by price.
The chart shows price decisively breaking through the last and highest demand zone, illustrating the concept that such zones can fail.

An Elliott Wave count is overlaid on the chart. Major impulse waves are labeled with red numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Sub-waves within the larger wave 3 are labeled with blue Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV, V). This visual aid introduces phase analysis.

The chart advances, showing price action after the peak of wave 5. Price has broken the demand zone and made a new low, but the candle wicks below the previous minor low create a 'bear trap' pattern, failing to close lower.
After the bear trap, the chart shows price moving back up and reclaiming the area of the previously violated demand zone. This zone now acts as support again.

An Andrews' Pitchfork is drawn using the pivots from waves 3, 4, and 5. The lower parallel line of the pitchfork is shown to align perfectly with the lows of the bear trap, providing a geometric support confluence.

A modified Schiff pitchfork is drawn using the same pivot points. Its lower parallel line is shown to precisely 'catch' the wicks of the bear trap candles, offering another layer of geometric confirmation.

The chart advances to its final state, showing that after the confirmed bear trap at the confluence of geometric and reclaimed zone support, the price rallied strongly, eventually exceeding the previous major high (wave 5).

semanticAnalysis.mainConcept: The core concept is that supply and demand zones are not infallible and require confirmation through confluent analysis before being trusted. The lesson demonstrates a multi-layered approach to determine if a zone will hold or fail by integrating: 1) Phase Analysis (Elliott Wave) to gauge market cycle exhaustion, 2) Candlestick Intrinsic Properties to read immediate buying/selling pressure, and 3) Minor Flow analysis to detect early shifts in trend, rather than relying solely on static, pre-drawn zones.
semanticAnalysis.deeperMeaning: The deeper implication is a critique of simplistic, mechanical trading based on static lines. It argues for a dynamic, contextual approach where the trader acts as a detective, gathering multiple, independent pieces of evidence (from market structure, cycles, candlestick behavior, and geometry) to build a high-probability thesis. The failure of a demand zone after a completed 5-wave impulse is presented not as a random event, but as a predictable outcome for a trader who understands market phases. The 'bear trap' scenario emphasizes that the most valuable information comes from how price *reacts* to a level, not the level itself.
semanticAnalysis.educationalGoal: The educational objective is to transition the trader from a basic understanding of support/resistance to an advanced, nuanced analysis of market turning points. The lesson aims to equip traders with a sophisticated toolkit to handle deceptive market scenarios where trends appear to be reversing but are actually setting up continuations (or vice-versa). By combining Elliott Wave, candlestick analysis, and minor flow, the video teaches a method to avoid being trapped by false breakouts and to identify high-probability entries when multiple analytical frameworks align.
